Dial
dī'al
n. (a graduated instrument marking the sun's shadow; the dial of Ahaz, on which the shadow went backward as a sign to Hezekiah)
From Latin dies, a day, through medieval Latin dialis. The Hebrew is maalah, a step or degree — the instrument was most likely a stair, and the shadow climbed or descended its steps.

Biblical Definition

Hezekiah, recovered from a mortal sickness, asked for a sign, and Isaiah offered him a choice: “This sign shalt thou have of the LORD, that the LORD will do the thing that he hath spoken: shall the shadow go forward ten degrees, or go back ten degrees?” (2 Kings 20:9). The king's reply shows he understood the difference: “It is a light thing for the shadow to go down ten degrees: nay, but let the shadow return backward ten degrees” (2 Kings 20:10). Forward is what shadows do; backward is not. “And Isaiah the prophet cried unto the LORD: and he brought the shadow ten degrees backward, by which it had gone down in the dial of Ahaz” (2 Kings 20:11). Isaiah records the same event with an added detail: “So the sun returned ten degrees, by which degrees it was gone down” (Isaiah 38:8). Two things are worth noticing. The instrument is named for Ahaz, Hezekiah's idolatrous father, so the sign was given on a device built by a wicked king. And the sign runs backward — the direction time does not go — to confirm a promise of fifteen added years.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a dial as an instrument for measuring time by the sun's shadow, consisting of a plate with lines and a gnomon or style.

expand to see more

DIAL, n. An instrument for measuring time by the aid of the sun; being a plate or plain surface, on which lines are drawn.

2. The plate of a clock or watch on which the hours are marked.

GNOMON, n. In dialing, the style or pin which by its shadow shows the hour of the day.

DEGREE, n. A step; a division of a line or space marked on an instrument.

SHADOW, n. Shade within defined limits; obscurity or deprivation of light, apparent on a plane.

Key Scripture

2 Kings 20:11 — "And Isaiah the prophet cried unto the LORD: and he brought the shadow ten degrees backward, by which it had gone down in the dial of Ahaz."

Isaiah 38:8 — "Behold, I will bring again the shadow of the degrees, which is gone down in the sun dial of Ahaz, ten degrees backward. So the sun returned ten degrees, by which degrees it was gone down."

2 Kings 20:9 — "And Isaiah said, This sign shalt thou have of the LORD, that the LORD will do the thing that he hath spoken: shall the shadow go forward ten degrees, or go back ten degrees?"

2 Kings 20:10 — "And Hezekiah answered, It is a light thing for the shadow to go down ten degrees: nay, but let the shadow return backward ten degrees."

Modern Corruption

The miracle is explained away as an optical curiosity, and the sign's point — a God who commands the shadow — is lost with it.

expand to see more

The standard treatment of this passage in critical commentary is to find a natural mechanism — a refraction, an eclipse, a local atmospheric effect — or to file the whole account as a later embellishment. Both moves assume in advance that the event as narrated cannot have occurred, which is the assumption itself and not a conclusion from evidence. The text is careful in a way that resists the reduction: Hezekiah is offered a choice, he reasons about which direction would constitute a sign, and he deliberately asks for the harder one. A narrative shaped to record an optical illusion would not include a king weighing which illusion to request.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is God's freedom over the order He established. Scripture never treats the regularity of creation as a limit on its Maker; the same God who appointed the sun to rule the day moved its shadow backward on a stairway in Jerusalem. This is why the resurrection is not, in biblical terms, an oddity requiring special pleading — it belongs to a God who has always dealt with His creation this way. The 1689 Confession states it: God in His ordinary providence makes use of means, yet is free to work without, above, and against them at His pleasure. The dial of Ahaz is that clause in a single afternoon.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew maalah, a step or degree — 2 Kings 20:9-11, Isaiah 38:8; tsel, a shadow — same passages; the instrument is called the degrees or steps of Ahaz.

expand to see more

Hebrew maalah — a step, stair, degree; rendered degrees and, in the construction, dial; the same word titles the Songs of Degrees.

Hebrew tsel — shadow; 2 Kings 20:9-11, the thing that moved.

Hebrew Ahaz — Hezekiah's father, an idolatrous king; the dial bore his name.

Hebrew oth — a sign; 2 Kings 20:9, what Hezekiah was given.

2 Chronicles 32:31 notes that the ambassadors of Babylon came to enquire of the wonder that was done in the land.

Usage

"“He brought the shadow ten degrees backward” — the direction shadows do not go."

"“It is a light thing for the shadow to go down” — Hezekiah asked for the harder sign."

"The sign was given on an instrument built by a wicked king."
